Keep the reason for failure separate from how the UI communicates it.

A failed request is both a pipeline event and a product communication problem. The application must preserve the reason a candidate was rejected while deciding whether to show a banner, record telemetry, or offer recovery. This chapter makes that distinction visible by simulating a failure without changing the normal CRUD requests.

Why this boundary matters

The pipeline owns error authority and finalization; the component observes the result and chooses how to present it. Clearing a global error acknowledges the current message but does not repair the failing condition. Keeping those responsibilities separate prevents UI feedback from becoming accidental pipeline control.

Use this structure for

  • validation failures that should prevent a candidate from committing
  • unavailable dependencies that need visible recovery guidance
  • authorization or operational failures that require monitoring

By the end of this chapter

You will be able to trigger a controlled pipeline failure, inspect its finalized error and snapshot, distinguish local emission from global error state, and restore normal CRUD behavior by resetting the cause.

Chapter 7 Starting Point and Failure Model

Start with the completed Chapter 6 project. This chapter changes the service, component, template, and specs. Normal CRUD calls remain unchanged so the pipeline—not the component—demonstrates failure and recovery.

Separate Four Responsibilities
  • The throwing filter creates the teaching failure.
  • The pipeline normalizes and finalizes the FeatureCell error.
  • errors() observes the feature-specific finalized error and snapshot.
  • VaultErrorService exposes application-level error state for presentation or monitoring.
Exceptions Are Not Routine Validation

This chapter throws deliberately so the Error stage is observable. Do not use unexpected exceptions as the default contract for ordinary form or domain validation. Use the library's documented rejection/validation mechanism for expected invalid input, and reserve exceptions for failures that should enter error handling.

Step 23: Simulate Pipeline Errors

↑ top

This chapter keeps the same service-owned and the same character workflow, but now you deliberately push one candidate path into the Error stage. The goal is not to change how add, edit, or delete are requested. The goal is to show what happens when the pipeline rejects those candidates before State can commit.

The existing pure removeUnknownLastNameFilter still runs first. After that, the service adds a second inline filter that normally returns the candidate unchanged. When the teaching flag is enabled, that inline filter throws intentionally. Because every create, update, and delete candidate flows through the same filter stage, all of those requests keep failing until you explicitly disable the simulated error.

Make the Change
  1. Open example.service.ts and register the pure filter, the intentional throwing filter, and the this.#vault.errors() callback.
  2. Keep the error callback observational only: capture the finalized error and immutable snapshot without changing error authority or pipeline control.
What to Look For
  • The simulated failure lives in the pipeline, not in the component. The component only triggers normal add, edit, and delete requests.
  • Once the teaching flag is enabled, every later mutation candidate keeps re-entering the same throwing filter until you reset it.
  • The errors() callback runs after the error has been normalized and committed as the finalized Vault error.
  • The callback receives the finalized error plus the immutable snapshot, but it does not mutate either one.

Step 24: Display Global Error State

↑ top

Now surface the failure in two separate teaching outputs. First, the component observes the singleton VaultErrorService so the UI can render the current global Vault error and clear it after acknowledgement. Second, the component renders the serialized output from the service-owned errors() callback so you can see the finalized error and snapshot that were emitted after error commitment.

Those two flows are related, but they are not the same thing. The global error service is independent of any one and works well for application-level concerns such as monitoring, banners, or shared recovery controls. The emitted error JSON is chapter-specific teaching output from this one fluent API registration.

Make the Change
  1. Open example.component.ts and subscribe to the singleton global error stream.
  2. Expose one action that clears the current global error and another action that disarms the simulated throwing filter.
  3. Update example.component.html so the page shows the global error banner, the Throw Error or Reset Error action, and the serialized errors() emission.
What to Look For
  • VaultErrorService is a singleton service, not a property of this chapter's .
  • Clicking Clear acknowledges the current global error, but it does not disable the simulated throwing filter.
  • Clicking Reset Error disables the filter and clears the global error without sending a new pipeline request.
  • The Error Emission textarea is populated by the errors() callback, not by the global error singleton.
Production Error Data

Render user-safe messages separately from diagnostic causes. Before sending an error or State snapshot to telemetry, redact credentials, personal data, and domain secrets; add correlation metadata outside the UI; and define whether retry repeats the request or first removes its failing condition. Clearing a banner is acknowledgement, not retry.

Error Representations and Consumers
Error representations, their consumers, and safe production content
Representation Consumer Safe content
Raw exception Normalization boundary Do not render or transmit without redaction.
VaultErrorShape Application error handling Normalized classification and approved context.
UI message User Actionable, non-sensitive summary.
Telemetry payload Operators Error code, feature key, and request ID—not the candidate.

Step 25: Complete Errors Tutorial

↑ top

The errors chapter is complete once you can enable the simulated filter failure, watch the global error banner appear, inspect the emitted error snapshot, and then prove that every later add, update, and delete candidate keeps failing while the filter remains enabled.

That final distinction matters. Clearing the global error acknowledges the current singleton error state, but it does not change why the next candidate will fail. The actual cause is still the enabled throwing filter in the pipeline. Once you reset that filter, the same feature resumes normal CRUD behavior without changing how the component requests work.

Run and Verify
  1. Click Throw Error to enable the simulated filter and send a candidate into the Error stage.
  2. Try one add, edit, or delete action while the button reads Reset Error and confirm the same pipeline failure keeps reappearing.
  3. Click Clear to acknowledge the active global error, then trigger another mutation to confirm the failure is still enabled.
  4. Click Reset Error and confirm later mutations succeed again through the normal service-owned boundary.
Errors Flow Summary
  • The tutorial now demonstrates how one throwing filter can stop later candidate commitment without changing the component's CRUD calls.
  • The singleton global error service provides application-level error visibility that is independent of any one .
  • The errors() fluent API provides a separate post-finalization observation surface for emitted error details.

Chapter 7 Exit Checkpoint

  • A teaching failure preserves the prior value and produces feature and global error observations.
  • Clearing presentation does not remove the cause; disabling the filter restores later requests.
  • Save this checkpoint for Chapter 8, which applies the same error model to async inputs.
